### A Field Guide to Small Things

There is a jar of basil cuttings on my kitchen counter, a rough Mason jar with water cloudy from neglect. The cuttings have been there for three weeks. I meant to plant them. The roots have finally grown into a soft white tangle, a small underwater forest that shifts whenever I refill the water. I have not planted them because I like the jar. I like how it turns a bright green growing thing into a strange suspended structure, roots like veins, stems like veins, a whole body of translucent in-between. I like how small it is. It asks for almost nothing, and I give it almost nothing, and still it makes roots.

I have been trying to learn how to be alive to small things. That sounds like something a self-help book would say, and I apologize. But I mean something less tidy. I mean the discipline of looking at a jar of basil for long enough that the looking becomes a kind of holding. I mean the way a cloud of roots can pull your attention out of the factory of your own head and give it back to you, cleaner, the way a tide returns a piece of glass that has been rolled and rolled until it is no longer sharp.

We live most of our lives at dashboard level. We scan the instrument cluster of our days: the red lights, the alerts, the unread counts, the temperature warnings, the fuel gauge, the little icons for Bluetooth and battery and weather. I am as guilty as anyone. I check my phone perhaps four hundred times a day, and I am not proud of that number; I only half-remember reading it in a study and then the number became its own tiny obsidian idol. I check it even when I don’t need to. I check it as if checking is a physical tic, a nervous twitch of the soul. The strange thing is that I have almost nothing urgent waiting for me. The infinite scroll is not the problem, and the problem is not the technology either. The problem is the attention itself, or what we let happen to it: we trade it, a few coins at a time, for pieces of what other people had for breakfast, for arguments with strangers who are not even arguing with us, for a series of little jolts that leave us tired but somehow also underfed.

My grandfather had a workshop at the back of his house, and the smell of it was sawdust, machine oil, and something like dried sweat. He fixed lamps and lawnmower engines, radios with cracked Bakelite cases, old coffee grinders, a grandfather clock that never kept time. I used to sit on the overturned milk crate and watch him do nothing. That is what I remember. The nothing. He would hold a bolt between his thumb and forefinger and look at it for a long time, as if the bolt might tell him where it belonged. He would turn a piece of metal over in his hand and read it the way another man might read a newspaper. Once, I asked him how he knew what was wrong with something. He said, “Because I listen to it.” I thought he was being silly. A lamp doesn’t make a sound. But he meant a different kind of listening. He meant paying attention to the details until they began to form the shape of the answer. He meant spending an afternoon on a single drill bit because the job deserves the job.

He died when I was thirteen, and I inherited a tool chest full of random things: screws sorted by no discernible logic, washers in a Tobacco tin, springs looking like tiny coiled snakes, a set of jeweler’s screwdrivers whose handles had the warm turning color of old bone. I don’t know how to fix anything. But I have kept the chest. I think I kept it as a reminder that there was once a kind of attention that did not need to be captured. It simply gave itself over, freely, like water taking the shape of a cup. I am not like that. My attention is a dog that runs off and comes back only when I have something to eat. But I am training it.

This is not a new complaint. People have been mourning their attention spans since the invention of the novel, or the pocket watch, or the alphabet. I know that. I know I am not special. But I also know that something about the current arrangement feels different in degree so vast that it becomes a difference in kind. The dashboard never dims. The alerts are designed by thousands of smart people in rooms full of beanbags and complicated coffee machines, and they are designed to feel like being needed. They are designed to make you worry. I worry, and then I check, and the checking settles the worry for about thirty seconds, and then the worry returns with a new shape, a new hunger. It is a machine for generating the sensation of being useful without ever being useful.

Meanwhile, the basil roots are growing. That is the important part. They are growing in water, in a jar, in a room where I live, and they do not care one bit about my productivity. They do not care about the email I have not answered or the article I have not finished. They do not care that I am behind on everything, that my to-do list stretches around the block and down the street and into a neighboring state. They are making roots, which is what they have always done, and will do, and they do it at their own pace. I find this almost unbearably moving. The basil is not trying to be anything. It is not shooting for its potential. It is not practicing gratitude or manifesting abundance. It is just being basil, and because it is being basil, it is doing the only holy thing it can do.

I have begun to take walks without an object. Or rather, with a different kind of object: not to get somewhere, not to be seen, not to rack up steps, but to see. I live in a city, so there is plenty to see if you are willing to look slowly. There is a man who waters the same patch of pavement outside his apartment every evening with a red watering can. There is a crack in the sidewalk that has become a delta system, braided and branching, and a tiny oak tree has taken root in it. The oak is about a foot high. It will probably be pulled out, or stepped on, or dried out, but for now it is a complete tree, made to scale, a bonsai of persistence. There is a coffee shop with a sign in the window that has said “Back in 5 minutes” for at least a year. There is a blue door I have never noticed before, even though I have walked past it a hundred times, and now I cannot unsee it. It is the blue of old toys, of my mother’s bathtub, of a certain kind of sky before dusk. It has a brass knocker shaped like a lion’s head, and the lion’s eyes are worn smooth as if by the touch of a million thumbs. But I am the one who touched it. I did. I walked up to the door and put my thumb on the lion’s eyes. I looked around afterward, embarrassed, but no one was watching. Everyone was looking at their own dashboard.

There is a word for this kind of walking. The French call it *flânerie*, but the word is too dressed up, too literary. I prefer the old Welsh word *cwtch*, which means both a cuddle and a small, hidden space. Or the Japanese *shinrin-yoku*, forest bathing, though I am urban and my bath is of concrete. Maybe there is a word in some language for the act of paying attention to the small, specific, useless particulars of being alive, and if there is, I want to live in that word. If there isn’t, I want to invent it. Let’s call it *the discipline of the blue door*. Every walk is an exercise in the discipline. Every street becomes a field guide. Every man with a watering can becomes a page. This is what my grandfather was doing in his workshop, I realize now. He was not fixing lamps. He was practicing a discipline. The lamp was just an excuse to have something to hold.

The strange thing is that when I pay attention, time changes. It stretches. A fifteen-minute walk can feel like an hour. A single basil cutting can hold an afternoon. Time is supposed to be money, but attention is the opposite: it spends and yet produces no wealth, or produces a different kind of wealth that has no price and cannot be displayed, and so we are told it is worthless. But what if worth is the wrong metric entirely? What if the point is not value but intimacy? What if the point is to be, for one small part of one small day, completely inside the present tense, like a root in water, like a thumb on a lion’s eye, like a man reading a bolt?

I have a friend who is a nurse, and she once told me that the dying do not ask for more time. They ask for meaning, for forgiveness, for the face of someone they love. And they often ask for water. Not for water in the abstract, but for a specific glass of water, a sip that tastes like a sip. She said that in her thirty years of working in hospice she never once heard someone say, “I wish I had checked my email more.” She did hear someone say, “I wish I had noticed the way the rain made the roses smell.” She heard a man who had been an engineer his whole life say that his greatest accomplishment was not a bridge but the apple tree he had planted outside his bedroom window. It had taken him forty years to realize it. The tree had been growing the whole time.

I think about that man a lot. Forty years. The tree was growing while he was at work, while he was earning promotions, while he was checking his watch, while he was doing the things that he thought were the things. And then one day he was dying, and the tree was outside his window, and it was the most important thing he had ever made. He didn’t make the tree exactly. He planted it. He watered it. He paid attention to it. That is the difference. He participated in its becoming, and the participation took almost no time at all. A hole, a sapling, a few buckets of water, a lifetime of looking up from the dashboard. That is all.

There is a concept in Celtic Christianity called “thin places,” places where the veil between the visible and the invisible is worn thin. I used to think those places were geographical, like the ruins of an island monastery or a hilltop with no trees. But I have begun to believe that thin places are not places at all. They are acts of attention. A thin place is a moment when you look at a basil root and see the entire architecture of life. A thin place is when the blue door becomes more real than the email. A thin place is when the man with the watering can is not a stranger but a fellow creature, holy in his pointless chore. The veil is always thin. We are the ones who are thick. We are the ones who have become insulated, dashboarded, wrapped in our own busyness. We are the ones who have made the veil thick with our own resistance.

I have been trying to practice resistance by doing almost nothing. I take a chair out to the small balcony and sit. I do not look at my phone. I do not listen to a podcast. I do not “use” the time for reflection or mindfulness or journaling. I just sit, the way my grandfather sat in his workshop, and I let the world come to me. At first it is terrible. My brain screams for stimulation. It wants the jolt. It is like a caffeine headache that will not stop. But after ten minutes, something softens. The traffic noise stops being noise and becomes a pattern. The motor hum of a refrigerator becomes a kind of chant. A pigeon lands on the railing. The pigeon is absurd. It bobs its head like a metronome. It eyes a stale crust of bread. I watch it for a long time. I watch it see the bread. I watch it decide. It walks around the bread, considers, pecks. It carries the bread away. I have never seen such a complete story.

Attention is not the same as love, but it is the root of it. You cannot love what you do not notice. You cannot care for what you do not see. And I wonder if the real crisis of our time is not loneliness or anxiety or polarization or any of the other words we use to describe the weather of our lives, but something more fundamental: the collapse of the faculty of wonder. We are losing the ability to be amazed by the ordinary. And if we lose that, we lose everything, because everything is ordinary. Everything. The birth of a child is an ordinary miracle; it happens at varying statistical rates in hospitals and homes around the world. The turning of the Earth is ordinary. The rise of a loaf of bread is a once-in-a-lifetime miracle that occurs three times a week in everyone’s kitchen. And the only way to see the miracle is to pay attention to it. To see it as if for the first time. To see it as if it were a blue door that was always there but you somehow never noticed.

I have been trying to write this piece, and I realize I have not once mentioned the basil since the beginning except to say it is still there. Let me check. Yes, it is still there. The water is cloudier, the roots are longer, and a new leaf has opened, a bright pale green, almost translucent at first, like a wing before it hardens. I have not planted the basil, and I think I never will. It has become a lesson. A few cuttings in a jar of water can sustain themselves for weeks, months even, as long as they have light and a little attention. They are not growing toward anything but more roots, more leaves, more basil. They are not trying to become a tomato plant. They are not envious of the spider plant on the shelf. They are completely, utterly themselves. That, I think, is the hardest thing in the world. Not to be extraordinary. To be ordinary. To be a person who is late, who is forgetful, who has a jar of basil cuttings on the counter and no plan to plant them, who takes walks and looks at blue doors, who sits on a balcony and watches a pigeon, and who calls that attendance. To be ordinary is to be accounted for, not in the ledgers of productivity, but in the small ongoing account of the world.

My grandfather’s workshop was a thin place. I see it now. The workbench was an altar. The topless tin of nails was a reliquary. The drill bits were saints. He was not a religious man, but he was deeply reverent, and his reverence was a matter of attention. He would not have explained it that way. If you had asked him about a lamp, he would have said, “It’s got a loose wire.” But that was a translation. The wire was not the problem. The problem was that the lamp had been neglected, that no one had looked at it closely enough, that the attention had broken. The lamp was a great teacher of attention disguised as a household object.

I am trying to be like that. I am trying to be a great teacher of attention disguised as nothing special. The basil jar teaches attention. The blue door teaches attention. The pigeon teaches attention, accidentally, by being exactly what it is. I want to be exactly what I am. But what am I? I am a person who gets distracted, who checks the phone, who loses the thread, who forgets. I am a person who sometimes looks up and sees the light falling on a wall and thinks, *that is enough*. I am a person who sometimes sits so long that the quiet begins to glow. And then I ruin it by thinking about how quiet it is, and then I am no longer in the quiet but talking about it, and that is the comedy and the tragedy and the whole business of being alive.

I have no grand conclusion. I have only the jar of basil. I am going to go look at it now. The roots will have grown a fraction of a fraction further. The water will be slightly cloudier. A leaf will have turned toward the window. The afternoon will have advanced. I will have missed a text. I will have lost nothing. I will have gained a moment that cannot be downloaded, cannot be liked, cannot be captured, cannot be sold. It will be mine only in the way a root is a root, only in the way a blue door is a blue door, only in the way a glass of water is a glass of water. That is enough. That is everything. That is the practice. I think my grandfather would have liked that. I think he would have grunted, which was his way of saying yes.

There is a jar of basil cuttings on my kitchen counter. I meant to plant them. I have not, and I will not. They are not supposed to be anywhere else. They are exactly where they belong, in water, in light, in a room where someone is trying, imperfectly, to pay attention. That is the only work. That is the whole work.
